theory.intro: The **area** of a rectangle is the amount of surface it covers. Multiply its length by its width.
facts: Area is measured in square units: cm$^2$, m$^2$, km$^2$.
A square is a rectangle with equal sides, so its area is **side $\times$ side**.
To compare rectangles, calculate each area first. Rectangles with different dimensions can have the same area.
Use the same length unit. Multiply the number of tiles in each row by the number of rows.
For paint or another covering, find the area first, then divide by the area covered by one litre or one piece.
steps: Read the length and the width (use the same unit for both).
Write the answer with squared units.

workedExamples.question_text: A rectangle is $7\text{ cm}$ long and $5\text{ cm}$ wide. Its length is increased by $2\text{ cm}$ and its width is decreased by $2\text{ cm}$. Find the new area and how much the area changes.
workedExamples.solution_text:
Original area
$A=7\times5$
$=35\text{ cm}^{2}$
New length: $7+2=9\text{ cm}$.
New width: $5-2=3\text{ cm}$.
New area
$A=9\times3$
$=27\text{ cm}^{2}$
$35-27=8\text{ cm}^{2}$
The area decreases by $8\text{ cm}^{2}$.

workedExamples.question_text: A rectangular floor is $5.6\text{ m}$ long and $2.7\text{ m}$ wide. Rectangular tiles are $40\text{ cm}$ long and $30\text{ cm}$ wide. The tiles are placed with their lengths along the length of the floor. How many tiles are needed?
workedExamples.solution_text:
Use centimetres for all the lengths.
$5.6\text{ m}=560\text{ cm}$ and $2.7\text{ m}=270\text{ cm}$.
$40\times14=560$, so $14$ tiles fit along the length.
$30\times9=270$, so $9$ rows fit across the width.
$14\times9=126$
$126$ tiles are needed.

workedExamples.question_text: A rectangular wall is $8\text{ m}$ long and $4.5\text{ m}$ high. One litre of paint covers $9\text{ m}^{2}$. How many litres are needed to paint the wall?
workedExamples.solution_text:
Area of the wall
$A=8\times4.5$
$=36\text{ m}^{2}$
$36\div9=4$
$4$ litres of paint are needed.

mastery.question_text:
A rectangle measures $6\text{ cm}$ by $5\text{ cm}$.
Both the length and the width are doubled.
Find the area of the new rectangle in $\text{cm}^{2}$, and state how many times as large it is as the original.
mastery.solution_text:
$A_{\text{old}}=6\times5$
$=30\text{ cm}^{2}$
New dimensions: $12\text{ cm}$ and $10\text{ cm}$.
$A_{\text{new}}=12\times10$
$=120\text{ cm}^{2}$
$120\div30=4$
The new area is $120\text{ cm}^{2}$, which is $4$ times the original.

mastery.question_text:
A rectangular courtyard is $12\text{ m}$ long and $7.5\text{ m}$ wide.
It is to be covered with rectangular pavers measuring $0.5\text{ m}$ by $0.3\text{ m}$.
How many pavers are needed?
mastery.solution_text:
Use centimetres for all the lengths.
$12\text{ m}=1200\text{ cm}$ and $7.5\text{ m}=750\text{ cm}$.
$0.5\text{ m}=50\text{ cm}$ and $0.3\text{ m}=30\text{ cm}$.
$50\times24=1200$, so $24$ pavers fit along the length.
$30\times25=750$, so $25$ rows fit across the width.
$24\times25=600$
$600$ pavers are needed.

mastery.question_text:
A rectangle has length $10\text{ cm}$ and width $6\text{ cm}$.
Its length is then increased by $2\text{ cm}$ and its width decreased by $2\text{ cm}$.
Find both areas in $\text{cm}^{2}$ and state whether the area is unchanged.
mastery.solution_text:
$A_{\text{old}}=10\times6$
$=60\text{ cm}^{2}$
$A_{\text{new}}=12\times4$
$=48\text{ cm}^{2}$
The area is not unchanged: it falls by $12\text{ cm}^{2}$.
